<reason>PRO built a cleaner, more consistent case: a memorable mechanism ("fix the water, not the swimmers"), concrete examples (Mexico tax, UK reformulation, Chile labels), and an equity argument that CON never once addressed across five speeches. PRO also executed the sharpest tactical move of the debate—when CON tried to disqualify environmental policy by demanding a "turning point" in Chile/Mexico, PRO absorbed CON's own individual-side examples (apps, coaching) into that same standard and showed none exist either, exposing in the closing that CON "abandons its own standard in the same paragraph" it invokes it. CON had real strengths—the compensation/whack-a-mole critique, the durability argument that regulation is perpetually re-litigated, and the "capacity travels with the person" frame—but left the abandonment-rate/dose-response point and the equity point unrebutted, and its opening was clipped for exceeding the word limit, costing it part of its collateral-cost argument. On balance PRO answered more of the live pressure and left fewer holes.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's turn in Rebuttal 2/Closing where it takes CON's own "name a country that bent the curve" standard from B1.1-B1.2, applies it symmetrically to CON's app/coaching evidence, and then in Closing catches CON quietly dropping that same standard once it cuts against CON ("abandons it in the same paragraph")—this exchange most decisively reframed who bore the unmet burden.</best_rebuttal>
